title: Renal Pharmacotherapeutics — Session 1

summary.text: Falling **GFR** makes renally cleared drugs **accumulate**: check CrCl first, then lower the maintenance dose, extend the interval, or both (loading doses often unchanged).
Each diuretic acts at one segment: **CAI/osmotic** proximal tubule, **loop** thick ascending limb, **thiazide** distal tubule, **K⁺-sparing** collecting duct.
**Loops** (NKCC2, ~25%) are most potent and **raise** urinary calcium; **thiazides** (NCC, ~5–8%) are first-line for hypertension and **lower** it.
Thiazides fade below **GFR ~30** — switch to a loop.
**Spironolactone/eplerenone** block the aldosterone receptor; **amiloride/triamterene** block ENaC; all risk **hyperkalemia**, worse with ACEi/ARB or CKD.
**Acetazolamide**: glaucoma, altitude sickness, alkalosis (causes acidosis). **Mannitol**: raised ICP/IOP; avoid in heart failure.

chunks.text: **Where diuretics act, and why renal function changes how every drug is dosed.** Renal physiology and pharmacokinetic principles set the dosing logic for everything that follows.
**The kidney is a major route of elimination for many drugs and active metabolites — renal function directly determines how long a drug stays in the body.**
Glomerular filtration rate (GFR) and creatinine clearance (CrCl) are the standard measures used to estimate renal drug-elimination capacity.

This is foundational Chapter 3 content applied specifically to the renal unit: renal dosing is not a separate topic but the lens through which every drug in this unit (and this course) should be viewed.

Digoxin, most antibiotics (e.g., vancomycin, many beta-lactams), many direct oral anticoagulants, metformin, and the diuretics covered later in this session are examples of drugs requiring renal dose adjustment.
Flow (Figure 1): GFR falls → renally cleared drug or active metabolite accumulates → toxicity.

**Figure 2. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): filtrate flows through the proximal tubule, thick ascending limb, distal convoluted tubule, and collecting duct — each diuretic class blocks sodium reabsorption at a different, specific segment.**
Share of filtered sodium reabsorbed: proximal tubule about 65%, thick ascending limb about 25%, distal tubule 5-8%, collecting duct 2-3% — this previews the potency ranking in Figure 7.
This nephron map is the conceptual spine of the session — every diuretic class is anchored back to its segment.
Match each diuretic class to the nephron segment where it acts: loop diuretics (furosemide) — thick ascending limb; thiazide diuretics (hydrochlorothiazide) — distal convoluted tubule.

Potassium-sparing — aldosterone antagonists (spironolactone) and ENaC blockers (amiloride) — collecting duct; carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (acetazolamide) — proximal tubule; osmotic diuretics (mannitol) — throughout.
CAI — proximal tubule; osmotic — acts osmotically throughout the filtrate-containing segments, mainly the proximal tubule and descending limb.
Renal tubule transport mechanisms: the proximal tubule reabsorbs about 66% of Na⁺ and 85% of NaHCO₃; organic acid secretion there delivers most diuretics to their luminal site.
Collecting tubule system: only 2–5% of NaCl, but where aldosterone acts and K⁺ is secreted; upstream diuretics deliver more Na⁺ here — the basis of diuretic K⁺ wasting.
Renal autacoids: adenosine (A1) lowers GFR; prostaglandins (PGE2) aid loop action; natriuretic peptides (nesiritide) and urodilatin cause natriuresis but have a limited clinical role.
Three levers: reduce the dose, extend the dosing interval, or both — the specific approach depends on the drug. Reduced GFR makes a renally cleared drug accumulate if unadjusted.
Reduce the maintenance dose when the drug’s effect is concentration-dependent; extend the dosing interval when the drug has a long half-life; monitor for toxicity after each dose change.
Loading doses are often unchanged; maintenance doses are what get adjusted.
As GFR falls, renally cleared drugs accumulate — dosing must be adjusted by reducing the dose, extending the interval, or both.
Active or toxic metabolites that are renally cleared matter just as much as the parent drug.

**Renal impairment also raises drug-interaction risk — drugs that are individually safe can become dangerous in combination when renal clearance is already reduced (a theme that returns explicitly in Session 2's "triple whammy" discussion).**
Pharmacokinetics in two numbers: volume of distribution links amount in the body to concentration; clearance links elimination rate to concentration.
Maintenance dose = clearance × target concentration (steady state depends only on clearance); loading dose = volume of distribution × target concentration, given slowly IV.
Drug accumulation: doses repeated more often than every four half-lives accumulate; steady state takes about four half-lives.
Check creatinine clearance before dosing any renally cleared drug (lower maintenance dose, extend the interval, or check CrCl) — especially in older adults.
Reassess as renal function changes — acute illness, dehydration, or new nephrotoxic drugs can drop GFR quickly.
When in doubt, consult dosing references or clinical pharmacy — this is not a "memorize every number" exercise; the point is the habit of checking renal function before dosing.
Distribution & clearance: adjust a renally cleared drug in proportion to creatinine clearance (Cockcroft-Gault; women 85% of the calculated value).
The target concentration strategy: choose a target, predict V and CL from weight and renal function, dose, measure the response, revise, repeat.
Dosing history: without it a drug level loses its predictive value; draw digoxin at least 6 hours after a dose.
Renal function determines drug dosing broadly, not just for diuretics — GFR/creatinine clearance should be checked before dosing any renally cleared drug (Chapter 3).
Textbook case: 85-year-old, 60 kg, CrCl 22 mL/min — digoxin clearance falls to 3.7 L/h, so about 127 mcg/day: two 62.5-mcg tablets.
What changes: Dose, interval, or both — depends on the drug · Practical consideration: Estimate CrCl or eGFR before dosing, especially in older adults
What changes: Loading dose often unchanged; maintenance dose adjusted · Practical consideration: Reassess when illness, dehydration or nephrotoxins drop GFR
What changes: Renally cleared active/toxic metabolites count too · Practical consideration: Use dosing references or clinical pharmacy
Why is the loading dose often unchanged? It fills the volume of distribution, which kidney failure doesn’t shrink much; clearance sets the maintenance dose.
**The two workhorse classes — one for potent natriuresis, one for everyday hypertension control.** They act on the thick ascending limb and the distal tubule.
Loops are the most potent class; thiazides are first-line for hypertension.
Furosemide, bumetanide, torsemide: loop diuretics. Hydrochlorothiazide: thiazide; chlorthalidone: thiazide-like.
**Mechanism: block the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter (NKCC2) in the thick ascending limb — the site responsible for ~25% of filtered sodium reabsorption.**

**Figure 3. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): loop diuretics block NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb, reducing Na+/Cl-/K+ reabsorption and collapsing the lumen-positive potential that normally drives paracellular calcium and magnesium reabsorption —**

**explaining the increased calcium and magnesium excretion seen with this class.** The lumen-positive potential (from K⁺ recycling) is the link students skip when they memorize “loops cause hypocalcemia” without the why.
**Mechanism: block the Na-Cl cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule — a less potent natriuretic site (~5–8% of filtered sodium) than the loop.**
Follow the thiazide chain step by step (Figure 4): NCC block in the DCT → sodium and water loss → lower intracellular sodium → calcium retained through the NCX exchanger → falling urinary calcium.
Contrast this with loop diuretics, which raise urinary calcium (Figure 3).

In one line: loop diuretics collapse the lumen-positive potential driving paracellular Ca²⁺/Mg²⁺ reabsorption (↑ excretion); thiazides increase distal calcium reabsorption through a separate mechanism (↓ excretion).
Loops work from the lumen, so their effect tracks proximal secretion; NSAIDs and probenecid compete and reduce it. NSAIDs also blunt the PGE2 contribution.
Loops: edema (heart failure, cirrhosis, renal disease) and, at times, hypertension when a thiazide alone is insufficient (e.g., significant renal impairment).
Loop diuretics increase calcium excretion — useful in hypercalcemia, and the opposite effect of thiazides.
Hydrochlorothiazide, chlorthalidone — first-line agents for essential hypertension; chlorthalidone has a longer half-life and is often preferred for 24-hour BP control.
Thiazides decrease calcium excretion — can be therapeutically useful in patients with osteoporosis and recurrent calcium-containing kidney stones.
Hypercalcemia: normal saline plus IV furosemide (80–120 mg) — a loop alone causes volume contraction and stops working.
Nephrolithiasis: thiazide plus more fluid and less salt; do not restrict dietary calcium.
Diabetes insipidus (nephrogenic, including lithium-induced): thiazides reduce polyuria; amiloride blocks lithium entry; monitor lithium levels.
Nonedematous states, hypertension: chlorthalidone lowers BP more than HCTZ but has more adverse effects; loops reserved for GFR < 30–40 mL/min or heart failure.
**Adverse effects: hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, metabolic alkalosis, ototoxicity (especially with rapid IV administration or high doses), and hyperuricemia.**
**Adverse effects: hyponatremia (can be significant, especially in older adults), hypokalemia, hyperglycemia, hyperuricemia (can precipitate gout), and hypercalcemia.**
Loops carry greater risk of ototoxicity and more pronounced electrolyte shifts than thiazides.
Thiazides: hyponatremia, gout, and hypokalemia are common adverse effects.
Thiazide hyperglycemia occurs at HCTZ > 50 mg/d, not at 12.5 mg/d or less; correcting hypokalemia partly reverses it.
Thiazides are the diuretics most associated with gout and cause hypomagnesemia more than loops; loop ototoxicity is usually reversible.
Risk of hyponatremia with different diuretic classes: thiazides highest (elderly women); loops protective (odds ratio 0.61).
Furosemide carries a sulfonamide-related structure — historical cross-reactivity concern with sulfa allergy, though the clinical risk is now considered low; still worth a careful allergy history.
Thiazides lose efficacy as GFR falls below approximately 30 mL/min — loop diuretics are generally preferred once renal function is significantly reduced.
Digoxin: hypokalemia from loops increases toxicity. Aminoglycosides: additive ototoxicity with loops.
Lithium: levels rise with thiazides. NSAIDs blunt the diuretic effect and raise AKI risk.
Diuretic combinations: loop agents and thiazides (often metolazone) are synergistic in loop resistance — but cause large fluid shifts and K⁺ wasting.
Chlorthalidone: long half-life of 40-60 hours.
Torsemide: longer half-life and more predictable absorption than furosemide. Bumetanide is about 40 times more potent than furosemide mg for mg.
Furosemide lasts 2–3 hours; torsemide 4–6 hours and absorbs in 1 hour, nearly as completely as IV. Torsemide is mainly cleared by the liver.
Chemistry & pharmacokinetics: all thiazides are sulfonamides given orally; chlorothiazide is the only parenteral thiazide.
Loops: monitor potassium, magnesium, creatinine. Thiazides: monitor sodium, potassium, calcium, glucose.
IV furosemide slowly (no faster than 4 mg/min) — ototoxicity with rapid IV or high doses.

The calcium-handling difference between loops and thiazides is one of the highest-yield comparison points in this whole unit: loops increase Ca2+ excretion, thiazides decrease it — state it both ways.

Case: hypertension and worsening CKD (eGFR now 25 mL/min), well controlled on chlorthalidone for years, but blood pressure has crept up. **What is the most likely explanation, and what change in therapy would you consider?**

**Thiazide diuretics lose much of their natriuretic efficacy once GFR falls below roughly 30 mL/min, because there is too little filtered sodium reaching the distal tubule for the drug to act on meaningfully.**
**A loop diuretic, which acts upstream at the thick ascending limb, remains effective even in advanced CKD and is the more appropriate choice here.**
The “thiazides lose efficacy in advanced CKD” point bridges directly to Session 2’s hypertension-in-CKD content.
Edematous states, heart failure: loops are standard, but overdiuresis cuts preload and cardiac output; hypokalemia worsens arrhythmias and digitalis toxicity.
Kidney disease and renal failure: little benefit below GFR 5 mL/min; high-dose loops or loop plus metolazone treat overload; avoid acetazolamide.
Textbook case: HCTZ added to chronic furosemide in CKD → 15 kg lost, BP 91/58, creatinine 10.8 — hypovolemic AKI; monitor closely, ideally inpatient.
Site, potency · Loop diuretics: Thick ascending limb — most potent natriuresis (~25%) · Thiazide diuretics: Distal convoluted tubule — modest natriuresis (~5–8%)
Calcium · Loop diuretics: Increase Ca²⁺ excretion · Thiazide diuretics: Decrease Ca²⁺ excretion
Best use · Loop diuretics: Preferred in edematous states and advanced CKD · Thiazide diuretics: First-line for essential hypertension with preserved renal function
Watch for · Loop diuretics: Greater risk of ototoxicity, more pronounced electrolyte shifts · Thiazide diuretics: Lose efficacy as GFR falls below ~30 mL/min

**Smaller in potency, but each with a distinct and important clinical niche.** Potassium-sparing, carbonic anhydrase inhibitor and osmotic diuretics act on the collecting duct and the proximal tubule.
**Two mechanistically distinct subgroups acting at the collecting duct, both reducing potassium and hydrogen ion secretion.**
Spironolactone, eplerenone: aldosterone receptor antagonists. Amiloride, triamterene: epithelial sodium channel (ENaC) blockers.
Carbonic anhydrase inhibitor: acetazolamide. Osmotic diuretic: mannitol.
Aldosterone binds the mineralocorticoid receptor → increases ENaC and Na/K pump activity → K+ and H+ secreted into the tubule. Blocking either step reduces potassium and hydrogen secretion.
Spironolactone and eplerenone block the receptor (block aldosterone’s effect directly); amiloride and triamterene block ENaC directly, independent of aldosterone.
**Acetazolamide (carbonic anhydrase inhibitor):** blocks Na+/HCO3- reabsorption in the proximal tubule → less HCO3- reabsorbed → bicarbonate diuresis, metabolic acidosis; weak diuretic effect.
**Mannitol (osmotic diuretic):** an inert, filtered but poorly reabsorbed solute that holds water in the tubule lumen osmotically — osmotic diuresis.
Side by side: acetazolamide removes bicarbonate reabsorption; mannitol removes water reabsorption by staying in the lumen. Both act before the loop, so their natriuretic potency is modest.
Figure 6 (**Schematic (illustrative)**): proximal tubule — carbonic anhydrase inhibition and osmotic holding of water (illustrative schematic).

**Figure 7. Original illustrative comparison (illustrative values, not from Katzung): loop diuretics block roughly 25% of filtered sodium reabsorption, substantially more than thiazides, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, or potassium-sparing diuretics —**
**directly reflecting the percentage normally reabsorbed at each nephron segment in Figure 2.** This is why loops are reached for first when potent natriuresis is the goal.
Potassium-sparing agents are often used in combination with a loop or thiazide diuretic specifically to offset potassium loss from the more potent class.
Acetazolamide: valued for non-diuretic uses — glaucoma (reduces aqueous humor production), altitude sickness prophylaxis, and metabolic alkalosis correction; also raised intracranial pressure.
Mannitol: used to reduce elevated intracranial or intraocular pressure and in certain cases of rhabdomyolysis-associated kidney injury prevention.
Know the niche, not an everyday use: acetazolamide = glaucoma/altitude sickness; mannitol = ICP/IOP reduction.
Potassium-sparing diuretics fit mineralocorticoid excess: primary (Conn syndrome) or secondary hyperaldosteronism (heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome).
Hepatic cirrhosis: resistant to loops but unusually responsive to spironolactone; aggressive diuresis risks hepatorenal syndrome and encephalopathy.
Renal & cardiac protection: aldosterone antagonists are cardioprotective and lower albuminuria; finerenone slowed CKD in type 2 diabetes.
Idiopathic edema (women 20–30): rule out surreptitious diuretic use; prefer moderate salt restriction.

**Primary adverse effect across the class: hyperkalemia — the risk rises sharply when combined with ACE inhibitors, ARBs, or in renal impairment (a direct preview of Session 2's cardiorenal drug-interaction content).**
Spironolactone also has antiandrogen effects (gynecomastia, menstrual irregularities) that eplerenone largely avoids.
Acetazolamide causes a mild metabolic acidosis as a predictable adverse effect, plus potassium loss; watch for kidney stones.
Mannitol expands extracellular volume — can worsen volume overload if used inappropriately; avoid it in heart failure and volume depletion.
K⁺-sparing agents can cause hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis (like type IV RTA); triamterene can cause kidney stones and, with indomethacin, acute renal failure.
Acetazolamide: drowsiness, paresthesias, calcium phosphate stones, hyperammonemia in cirrhosis; monitor potassium and phosphorus.
Mannitol: early ECF expansion and hyponatremia, later dehydration, hypernatremia and hyperkalemia; AKI in 6–7% of patients.
Mannitol requires intact renal perfusion to be effective.
Eplerenone: avoid with potassium above 5.5 mEq/L, CrCl below 30 mL/min, or strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (such as ketoconazole).
Hyperkalemia risk rises with ACE inhibitors, ARBs, or CKD — both block aldosterone’s effect, so the classes are combined carefully.
Flag the hyperkalemia-with-ACEi/ARB interaction as a preview: this exact combination becomes a major theme in Session 2 when RAAS blockers are introduced.
Potassium supplements and trimethoprim: hyperkalemia with potassium-sparing diuretics.
Sulfonamide allergy: caution with loops, thiazides, acetazolamide. Metformin, vancomycin, DOACs: renally cleared; need dose adjustment.
Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (erythromycin, fluconazole, diltiazem, grapefruit juice) raise eplerenone but not spironolactone levels.
RALES showed spironolactone helps severe heart failure on an ACE inhibitor — afterward hyperkalemia admissions and deaths rose.
Acetazolamide diuresis fades within 2–3 days (reduce dose in renal insufficiency); mannitol must be given IV — orally it causes osmotic diarrhea.
Spironolactone: monitor potassium and creatinine within 1 week; life-threatening hyperkalemia, especially in CKD or with ACE inhibitor/ARB.
Mannitol: monitor osmolality and electrolytes.

Case: a patient with stage 3 chronic kidney disease and heart failure is taking an ACE inhibitor and is started on spironolactone for additional heart-failure benefit; two weeks later a routine basic metabolic panel shows potassium 6.1 mEq/L.
**What is the mechanistic explanation for this finding, and what does it suggest about future drug combinations in this unit?**

**Both the ACE inhibitor (by reducing aldosterone) and spironolactone (by directly blocking the aldosterone receptor) independently reduce potassium excretion — combined, and in the setting of CKD (which already impairs potassium excretion), the hyperkalemia risk compounds.**
**This is the same additive-risk logic that will reappear as the "triple whammy" in Session 2.** The ACEi/aldosterone-antagonist pair is one of three “whammies” formalized next session.

Recap: diuretic classes are organized by nephron site (Figure 2): loop diuretics (thick ascending limb) are most potent, followed by thiazides (distal tubule), then potassium-sparing and carbonic anhydrase inhibitors.
Recap: loop and thiazide diuretics have opposite effects on calcium excretion (Figure 3); potassium-sparing diuretics carry a hyperkalemia risk that compounds with ACE inhibitors or ARBs.

Session 2 (Thursday, November 19) continues with antihypertensive therapy in chronic kidney disease and the cardiovascular-renal overlap, including vasodilators and angina pharmacology — RAAS blockers and the triple whammy first.
SGLT2 inhibitors block proximal glucose and Na⁺ reabsorption; main indication now cardiorenal protection. Adverse reactions: sixfold genital fungal infections in women, initial GFR dip.
Antidiuretic hormone antagonists (vaptans): oral tolvaptan (V2), IV conivaptan (V1a and V2) for SIADH when water restriction fails; watch sodium and liver tests.

1.title: Renal Pharmacotherapeutics
1.notes:
Instructor script:

Say: "Two ideas run through this unit. First, the kidney clears many drugs, so renal function changes dosing."

2.title: Learning Objectives — Session 1
2.notes:
Orient students to the arc of this session: renal physiology and dosing principles first, then the five diuretic classes organized by where they act along the nephron. Session 2 builds directly on this foundation — RAAS-blocking antihypertensives are, mechanistically, the natural next step after today's diuretic content.

Instructor script:

Say: "Second, every diuretic works at one specific nephron segment, and that location predicts its effects, its adverse effects and its interactions."

3.title: Required & Recommended Readings — Unit 5
3.notes:
Point students to the required readings for today — Chapters 15 and 3 — and flag that Chapters 11 and 12 are supplemental reading specifically for Session 2, where they will frame hypertension management in CKD and the cardiorenal overlap with angina pharmacology.

Instructor script:

Readings: Katzung chapters 15 and 3 for today; chapters 11 and 12 are supplemental for Session 2.

4.notes:
Section transition.

Renal physiology and pharmacokinetic principles set the dosing logic for everything that follows.

5.title: Renal Drug Clearance and Dosing
5.notes:
This is foundational Chapter 3 content applied specifically to the renal unit — the goal is for students to see renal dosing not as a separate topic but as the lens through which every other drug in this unit (and this course) should be viewed.

Instructor script:

GFR and creatinine clearance estimate elimination capacity. As GFR falls, renally cleared drugs accumulate. Examples: vancomycin, many beta-lactams, digoxin, DOACs, metformin.

6.title: Renal Dose Adjustment: Dose, Interval, or Both
6.notes:
Walk the flow from falling GFR to toxicity, then ask students which lever to pull: dose, interval, or both. This sets up the renal dosing content that follows.

Instructor script:

Walk the flow: GFR falls, drug or active metabolite accumulates, toxicity. Fixes: lower the maintenance dose, extend the interval, or both. Loading doses are often unchanged.

7.title: Diuretic Sites of Action Along the Nephron
7.notes:
This is the conceptual spine for the rest of the session — every diuretic class that follows gets anchored back to its segment on this diagram. Point out that the percentage of filtered sodium normally reabsorbed at each site previews the potency ranking in Figure 7.

Instructor script:

Name the segment and the share of filtered sodium: proximal tubule about 65%, thick ascending limb about 25%, distal tubule 5-8%, collecting duct 2-3%.

8.title: Dosing Adjustment in Renal Impairment
8.notes:
Keep this practical rather than exhaustive — the point is the habit of checking renal function before dosing, not memorizing specific adjustment tables for every drug.

Instructor script:

Know: Estimate CrCl or eGFR before dosing; reassess when illness, dehydration or nephrotoxic drugs change GFR.

9.notes:
Section transition.

Loop and thiazide diuretics are the two classes that act on the thick ascending limb and the distal tubule.

10.title: Loop Diuretics
10.notes:
The calcium-handling difference between loops and thiazides is one of the highest-yield comparison points in this whole unit — make sure students can state it both ways (loops increase Ca2+ excretion, thiazides decrease it) before moving to Figure 2.

Instructor script:

Furosemide, bumetanide, torsemide block NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb. Most potent. Adverse effects: hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, metabolic alkalosis, ototoxicity, hyperuricemia.

Know: Increase calcium excretion (useful in hypercalcemia). Sulfonamide allergy cross-reactivity is low.

11.title: The Na-K-2Cl Cotransporter (NKCC2): Loop Diuretic Target
11.notes:
Walk the diagram left to right, then down to the K+ recycling box — the lumen-positive potential is the mechanistic link between NKCC2 blockade and increased Ca2+/Mg2+ excretion. This is the piece students most often skip when they memorize "loops cause hypocalcemia" without understanding why.

Instructor script:

Left to right, then the potassium recycling box. Blocking NKCC2 collapses the lumen-positive potential that drives paracellular calcium and magnesium reabsorption.

12.title: Thiazide Diuretics
12.notes:
The "thiazides lose efficacy in advanced CKD" point sets up a direct bridge to Session 2's hypertension-in-CKD content — flag that connection explicitly here.

Instructor script:

Block NCC in the distal tubule. First-line in hypertension. Adverse effects: hyponatremia, hypokalemia, hyperglycemia, hyperuricemia, hypercalcemia. Lose efficacy at GFR below about 30.

13.title: Thiazides: Distal Tubule NCC Block and Calcium Reabsorption
13.notes:
Students should follow the chain step by step: NCC block, sodium loss, lower intracellular sodium, calcium retained through the exchanger, and falling urinary calcium. Contrast this with loop diuretics, which raise urinary calcium (Figure 3).

Instructor script:

NCC block lowers intracellular sodium, which favors NCX calcium reabsorption, so urinary calcium falls. Useful for calcium stones and osteoporosis.

14.title: Loop vs. Thiazide Diuretics
14.notes:
Use this slide as the consolidating recap before the case — students should be able to generate this table from memory by the end of the unit.

Instructor script:

Students should reproduce this table from memory.

15.title: Choosing a Diuretic for Advancing CKD
15.notes:
This case makes the loop-vs-thiazide GFR cutoff concrete and clinical rather than an isolated fact to memorize — a good checkpoint before the quick check.

Instructor script:

At eGFR 25 a thiazide has too little filtrate to act on; switch to a loop.

16.notes:
Section transition.

Potassium-sparing, carbonic anhydrase inhibitor and osmotic diuretics act on the collecting duct and the proximal tubule.

17.title: Potassium-Sparing Diuretics
17.notes:
Flag the hyperkalemia-with-ACEi/ARB interaction explicitly as a preview — this exact combination becomes a major theme in Session 2 when RAAS blockers are introduced.

Instructor script:

Aldosterone antagonists (spironolactone, eplerenone) and ENaC blockers (amiloride, triamterene). Hyperkalemia is the main risk, especially with ACE inhibitors, ARBs and CKD.

18.title: Collecting Duct: Aldosterone Blockers vs. ENaC Blockers
18.notes:
Anchor the two classes to the same segment: one blocks the hormone's receptor, the other blocks the channel the hormone turns on. Both raise potassium when used alone, which is why they are combined carefully with ACE inhibitors and ARBs.

Instructor script:

Aldosterone drives ENaC and the sodium-potassium pump; blocking either reduces potassium and hydrogen secretion.

19.title: Carbonic Anhydrase Inhibitors & Osmotic Diuretics
19.notes:
Both of these classes are "know the niche use, not the everyday one" — students should walk away knowing acetazolamide = glaucoma/altitude sickness and mannitol = ICP/IOP reduction, more than thinking of either as a mainstream diuretic.

Instructor script:

Acetazolamide for glaucoma, altitude sickness and alkalosis. Mannitol for raised ICP and IOP.

20.title: Proximal Tubule: Acetazolamide and Mannitol
20.notes:
Explain the two proximal mechanisms side by side: acetazolamide removes bicarbonate reabsorption, mannitol removes water reabsorption by staying in the lumen. Both act before the loop, which is why their effect is modest in natriuretic potency.

Instructor script:

Bicarbonate diuresis with metabolic acidosis; mannitol holds water in the lumen and needs renal perfusion.

U5-R1.question: Why does declining renal function (falling GFR) change how a renally-cleared drug must be dosed? Name two parameters that might be adjusted.
U5-R1.answer: Reduced GFR causes a renally-cleared drug to accumulate if unadjusted; reduce the dose, extend the interval, or both.

U5-R2.question: List the five diuretic classes covered and the nephron segment where each one acts.
U5-R2.answer: Loop — thick ascending limb; thiazide — distal convoluted tubule; potassium-sparing — collecting duct; CAI — proximal tubule; osmotic — acts osmotically throughout the filtrate-containing segments.

U5-R3.question: Why do loop diuretics increase calcium excretion while thiazide diuretics decrease it?
U5-R3.answer: Loop diuretics collapse the lumen-positive potential driving paracellular Ca²⁺/Mg²⁺ reabsorption (↑ excretion); thiazides increase distal calcium reabsorption through a separate mechanism (↓ excretion).

U5-R4.question: Compare the clinical niches of loop vs. thiazide diuretics. At roughly what GFR do thiazides lose much of their natriuretic efficacy, and what should be considered instead?
U5-R4.answer: Loop — most potent, edematous states/advanced CKD; thiazide — first-line HTN with preserved renal function, loses efficacy below ~30 mL/min (switch to a loop).

U5-R5.question: Name the two mechanistically distinct subgroups of potassium-sparing diuretics, with one example of each. What is the shared major adverse effect across this class, and what raises its risk sharply?
U5-R5.answer: Aldosterone antagonists (spironolactone, eplerenone) and ENaC blockers (amiloride, triamterene); shared risk — hyperkalemia, worsened by ACEi/ARB or renal impairment.

U5-R6.question: What is the mechanism of acetazolamide, and name two of its non-diuretic clinical uses.
U5-R6.answer: Blocks Na⁺/HCO₃⁻ reabsorption in the proximal tubule; used for glaucoma and altitude sickness prophylaxis.

children.name: Class
facts: **Where diuretics act, and why renal function changes how every drug is dosed.** Renal physiology and pharmacokinetic principles set the dosing logic for everything that follows.
**The kidney is a major route of elimination for many drugs and active metabolites — renal function directly determines how long a drug stays in the body.**
Glomerular filtration rate (GFR) and creatinine clearance (CrCl) are the standard measures used to estimate renal drug-elimination capacity.

This is foundational Chapter 3 content applied specifically to the renal unit: renal dosing is not a separate topic but the lens through which every drug in this unit (and this course) should be viewed.

children.name: Prototype + other drugs named
facts: Digoxin, most antibiotics (e.g., vancomycin, many beta-lactams), many direct oral anticoagulants, metformin, and the diuretics covered later in this session are examples of drugs requiring renal dose adjustment.

children.name: Mechanism of action
facts: Flow (Figure 1): GFR falls → renally cleared drug or active metabolite accumulates → toxicity.

**Figure 2. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): filtrate flows through the proximal tubule, thick ascending limb, distal convoluted tubule, and collecting duct — each diuretic class blocks sodium reabsorption at a different, specific segment.**
Share of filtered sodium reabsorbed: proximal tubule about 65%, thick ascending limb about 25%, distal tubule 5-8%, collecting duct 2-3% — this previews the potency ranking in Figure 7.
This nephron map is the conceptual spine of the session — every diuretic class is anchored back to its segment.
Match each diuretic class to the nephron segment where it acts: loop diuretics (furosemide) — thick ascending limb; thiazide diuretics (hydrochlorothiazide) — distal convoluted tubule.

Potassium-sparing — aldosterone antagonists (spironolactone) and ENaC blockers (amiloride) — collecting duct; carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (acetazolamide) — proximal tubule; osmotic diuretics (mannitol) — throughout.
CAI — proximal tubule; osmotic — acts osmotically throughout the filtrate-containing segments, mainly the proximal tubule and descending limb.
Renal tubule transport mechanisms: the proximal tubule reabsorbs about 66% of Na⁺ and 85% of NaHCO₃; organic acid secretion there delivers most diuretics to their luminal site.
Collecting tubule system: only 2–5% of NaCl, but where aldosterone acts and K⁺ is secreted; upstream diuretics deliver more Na⁺ here — the basis of diuretic K⁺ wasting.
Renal autacoids: adenosine (A1) lowers GFR; prostaglandins (PGE2) aid loop action; natriuretic peptides (nesiritide) and urodilatin cause natriuresis but have a limited clinical role.

children.name: Indications
facts: Three levers: reduce the dose, extend the dosing interval, or both — the specific approach depends on the drug. Reduced GFR makes a renally cleared drug accumulate if unadjusted.
Reduce the maintenance dose when the drug’s effect is concentration-dependent; extend the dosing interval when the drug has a long half-life; monitor for toxicity after each dose change.
Loading doses are often unchanged; maintenance doses are what get adjusted.

children.name: Adverse effects (boxed warnings first)
facts: As GFR falls, renally cleared drugs accumulate — dosing must be adjusted by reducing the dose, extending the interval, or both.
Active or toxic metabolites that are renally cleared matter just as much as the parent drug.

children.name: Drug interactions
facts: **Renal impairment also raises drug-interaction risk — drugs that are individually safe can become dangerous in combination when renal clearance is already reduced (a theme that returns explicitly in Session 2's "triple whammy" discussion).**

children.name: Pharmacokinetics
facts: Pharmacokinetics in two numbers: volume of distribution links amount in the body to concentration; clearance links elimination rate to concentration.
Maintenance dose = clearance × target concentration (steady state depends only on clearance); loading dose = volume of distribution × target concentration, given slowly IV.
Drug accumulation: doses repeated more often than every four half-lives accumulate; steady state takes about four half-lives.

children.name: Monitoring
facts: Check creatinine clearance before dosing any renally cleared drug (lower maintenance dose, extend the interval, or check CrCl) — especially in older adults.
Reassess as renal function changes — acute illness, dehydration, or new nephrotoxic drugs can drop GFR quickly.
When in doubt, consult dosing references or clinical pharmacy — this is not a "memorize every number" exercise; the point is the habit of checking renal function before dosing.
Distribution & clearance: adjust a renally cleared drug in proportion to creatinine clearance (Cockcroft-Gault; women 85% of the calculated value).
The target concentration strategy: choose a target, predict V and CL from weight and renal function, dose, measure the response, revise, repeat.
Dosing history: without it a drug level loses its predictive value; draw digoxin at least 6 hours after a dose.

children.name: Clinical pearls / "why" hook
facts: Renal function determines drug dosing broadly, not just for diuretics — GFR/creatinine clearance should be checked before dosing any renally cleared drug (Chapter 3).
Textbook case: 85-year-old, 60 kg, CrCl 22 mL/min — digoxin clearance falls to 3.7 L/h, so about 127 mcg/day: two 62.5-mcg tablets.

children.name: Class
facts: **The two workhorse classes — one for potent natriuresis, one for everyday hypertension control.** They act on the thick ascending limb and the distal tubule.
Loops are the most potent class; thiazides are first-line for hypertension.

children.name: Prototype + other drugs named
facts: Furosemide, bumetanide, torsemide: loop diuretics. Hydrochlorothiazide: thiazide; chlorthalidone: thiazide-like.

children.name: Mechanism of action
facts: **Mechanism: block the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter (NKCC2) in the thick ascending limb — the site responsible for ~25% of filtered sodium reabsorption.**

**Figure 3. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): loop diuretics block NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb, reducing Na+/Cl-/K+ reabsorption and collapsing the lumen-positive potential that normally drives paracellular calcium and magnesium reabsorption —**

**explaining the increased calcium and magnesium excretion seen with this class.** The lumen-positive potential (from K⁺ recycling) is the link students skip when they memorize “loops cause hypocalcemia” without the why.
**Mechanism: block the Na-Cl cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule — a less potent natriuretic site (~5–8% of filtered sodium) than the loop.**
Follow the thiazide chain step by step (Figure 4): NCC block in the DCT → sodium and water loss → lower intracellular sodium → calcium retained through the NCX exchanger → falling urinary calcium.
Contrast this with loop diuretics, which raise urinary calcium (Figure 3).

In one line: loop diuretics collapse the lumen-positive potential driving paracellular Ca²⁺/Mg²⁺ reabsorption (↑ excretion); thiazides increase distal calcium reabsorption through a separate mechanism (↓ excretion).
Loops work from the lumen, so their effect tracks proximal secretion; NSAIDs and probenecid compete and reduce it. NSAIDs also blunt the PGE2 contribution.

children.name: Indications
facts: Loops: edema (heart failure, cirrhosis, renal disease) and, at times, hypertension when a thiazide alone is insufficient (e.g., significant renal impairment).
Loop diuretics increase calcium excretion — useful in hypercalcemia, and the opposite effect of thiazides.
Hydrochlorothiazide, chlorthalidone — first-line agents for essential hypertension; chlorthalidone has a longer half-life and is often preferred for 24-hour BP control.
Thiazides decrease calcium excretion — can be therapeutically useful in patients with osteoporosis and recurrent calcium-containing kidney stones.
Hypercalcemia: normal saline plus IV furosemide (80–120 mg) — a loop alone causes volume contraction and stops working.
Nephrolithiasis: thiazide plus more fluid and less salt; do not restrict dietary calcium.
Diabetes insipidus (nephrogenic, including lithium-induced): thiazides reduce polyuria; amiloride blocks lithium entry; monitor lithium levels.
Nonedematous states, hypertension: chlorthalidone lowers BP more than HCTZ but has more adverse effects; loops reserved for GFR < 30–40 mL/min or heart failure.

children.name: Adverse effects (boxed warnings first)
facts: **Adverse effects: hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, metabolic alkalosis, ototoxicity (especially with rapid IV administration or high doses), and hyperuricemia.**
**Adverse effects: hyponatremia (can be significant, especially in older adults), hypokalemia, hyperglycemia, hyperuricemia (can precipitate gout), and hypercalcemia.**
Loops carry greater risk of ototoxicity and more pronounced electrolyte shifts than thiazides.
Thiazides: hyponatremia, gout, and hypokalemia are common adverse effects.
Thiazide hyperglycemia occurs at HCTZ > 50 mg/d, not at 12.5 mg/d or less; correcting hypokalemia partly reverses it.
Thiazides are the diuretics most associated with gout and cause hypomagnesemia more than loops; loop ototoxicity is usually reversible.
Risk of hyponatremia with different diuretic classes: thiazides highest (elderly women); loops protective (odds ratio 0.61).

children.name: Contraindications
facts: Furosemide carries a sulfonamide-related structure — historical cross-reactivity concern with sulfa allergy, though the clinical risk is now considered low; still worth a careful allergy history.
Thiazides lose efficacy as GFR falls below approximately 30 mL/min — loop diuretics are generally preferred once renal function is significantly reduced.

children.name: Drug interactions
facts: Digoxin: hypokalemia from loops increases toxicity. Aminoglycosides: additive ototoxicity with loops.
Lithium: levels rise with thiazides. NSAIDs blunt the diuretic effect and raise AKI risk.
Diuretic combinations: loop agents and thiazides (often metolazone) are synergistic in loop resistance — but cause large fluid shifts and K⁺ wasting.

children.name: Pharmacokinetics
facts: Chlorthalidone: long half-life of 40-60 hours.
Torsemide: longer half-life and more predictable absorption than furosemide. Bumetanide is about 40 times more potent than furosemide mg for mg.
Furosemide lasts 2–3 hours; torsemide 4–6 hours and absorbs in 1 hour, nearly as completely as IV. Torsemide is mainly cleared by the liver.
Chemistry & pharmacokinetics: all thiazides are sulfonamides given orally; chlorothiazide is the only parenteral thiazide.

children.name: Monitoring
facts: Loops: monitor potassium, magnesium, creatinine. Thiazides: monitor sodium, potassium, calcium, glucose.
IV furosemide slowly (no faster than 4 mg/min) — ototoxicity with rapid IV or high doses.

children.name: Clinical pearls / "why" hook
facts: The calcium-handling difference between loops and thiazides is one of the highest-yield comparison points in this whole unit: loops increase Ca2+ excretion, thiazides decrease it — state it both ways.

Case: hypertension and worsening CKD (eGFR now 25 mL/min), well controlled on chlorthalidone for years, but blood pressure has crept up. **What is the most likely explanation, and what change in therapy would you consider?**

**Thiazide diuretics lose much of their natriuretic efficacy once GFR falls below roughly 30 mL/min, because there is too little filtered sodium reaching the distal tubule for the drug to act on meaningfully.**
**A loop diuretic, which acts upstream at the thick ascending limb, remains effective even in advanced CKD and is the more appropriate choice here.**
The “thiazides lose efficacy in advanced CKD” point bridges directly to Session 2’s hypertension-in-CKD content.
Edematous states, heart failure: loops are standard, but overdiuresis cuts preload and cardiac output; hypokalemia worsens arrhythmias and digitalis toxicity.
Kidney disease and renal failure: little benefit below GFR 5 mL/min; high-dose loops or loop plus metolazone treat overload; avoid acetazolamide.
Textbook case: HCTZ added to chronic furosemide in CKD → 15 kg lost, BP 91/58, creatinine 10.8 — hypovolemic AKI; monitor closely, ideally inpatient.

children.name: Class
facts: **Smaller in potency, but each with a distinct and important clinical niche.** Potassium-sparing, carbonic anhydrase inhibitor and osmotic diuretics act on the collecting duct and the proximal tubule.
**Two mechanistically distinct subgroups acting at the collecting duct, both reducing potassium and hydrogen ion secretion.**

children.name: Prototype + other drugs named
facts: Spironolactone, eplerenone: aldosterone receptor antagonists. Amiloride, triamterene: epithelial sodium channel (ENaC) blockers.
Carbonic anhydrase inhibitor: acetazolamide. Osmotic diuretic: mannitol.

children.name: Mechanism of action
facts: Aldosterone binds the mineralocorticoid receptor → increases ENaC and Na/K pump activity → K+ and H+ secreted into the tubule. Blocking either step reduces potassium and hydrogen secretion.
Spironolactone and eplerenone block the receptor (block aldosterone’s effect directly); amiloride and triamterene block ENaC directly, independent of aldosterone.
**Acetazolamide (carbonic anhydrase inhibitor):** blocks Na+/HCO3- reabsorption in the proximal tubule → less HCO3- reabsorbed → bicarbonate diuresis, metabolic acidosis; weak diuretic effect.
**Mannitol (osmotic diuretic):** an inert, filtered but poorly reabsorbed solute that holds water in the tubule lumen osmotically — osmotic diuresis.
Side by side: acetazolamide removes bicarbonate reabsorption; mannitol removes water reabsorption by staying in the lumen. Both act before the loop, so their natriuretic potency is modest.
Figure 6 (**Schematic (illustrative)**): proximal tubule — carbonic anhydrase inhibition and osmotic holding of water (illustrative schematic).

**Figure 7. Original illustrative comparison (illustrative values, not from Katzung): loop diuretics block roughly 25% of filtered sodium reabsorption, substantially more than thiazides, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, or potassium-sparing diuretics —**
**directly reflecting the percentage normally reabsorbed at each nephron segment in Figure 2.** This is why loops are reached for first when potent natriuresis is the goal.

children.name: Indications
facts: Potassium-sparing agents are often used in combination with a loop or thiazide diuretic specifically to offset potassium loss from the more potent class.
Acetazolamide: valued for non-diuretic uses — glaucoma (reduces aqueous humor production), altitude sickness prophylaxis, and metabolic alkalosis correction; also raised intracranial pressure.
Mannitol: used to reduce elevated intracranial or intraocular pressure and in certain cases of rhabdomyolysis-associated kidney injury prevention.
Know the niche, not an everyday use: acetazolamide = glaucoma/altitude sickness; mannitol = ICP/IOP reduction.
Potassium-sparing diuretics fit mineralocorticoid excess: primary (Conn syndrome) or secondary hyperaldosteronism (heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome).
Hepatic cirrhosis: resistant to loops but unusually responsive to spironolactone; aggressive diuresis risks hepatorenal syndrome and encephalopathy.
Renal & cardiac protection: aldosterone antagonists are cardioprotective and lower albuminuria; finerenone slowed CKD in type 2 diabetes.
Idiopathic edema (women 20–30): rule out surreptitious diuretic use; prefer moderate salt restriction.

children.name: Adverse effects (boxed warnings first)
facts: **Primary adverse effect across the class: hyperkalemia — the risk rises sharply when combined with ACE inhibitors, ARBs, or in renal impairment (a direct preview of Session 2's cardiorenal drug-interaction content).**
Spironolactone also has antiandrogen effects (gynecomastia, menstrual irregularities) that eplerenone largely avoids.
Acetazolamide causes a mild metabolic acidosis as a predictable adverse effect, plus potassium loss; watch for kidney stones.
Mannitol expands extracellular volume — can worsen volume overload if used inappropriately; avoid it in heart failure and volume depletion.
K⁺-sparing agents can cause hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis (like type IV RTA); triamterene can cause kidney stones and, with indomethacin, acute renal failure.
Acetazolamide: drowsiness, paresthesias, calcium phosphate stones, hyperammonemia in cirrhosis; monitor potassium and phosphorus.
Mannitol: early ECF expansion and hyponatremia, later dehydration, hypernatremia and hyperkalemia; AKI in 6–7% of patients.

children.name: Contraindications
facts: Mannitol requires intact renal perfusion to be effective.
Eplerenone: avoid with potassium above 5.5 mEq/L, CrCl below 30 mL/min, or strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (such as ketoconazole).

children.name: Drug interactions
facts: Hyperkalemia risk rises with ACE inhibitors, ARBs, or CKD — both block aldosterone’s effect, so the classes are combined carefully.
Flag the hyperkalemia-with-ACEi/ARB interaction as a preview: this exact combination becomes a major theme in Session 2 when RAAS blockers are introduced.
Potassium supplements and trimethoprim: hyperkalemia with potassium-sparing diuretics.
Sulfonamide allergy: caution with loops, thiazides, acetazolamide. Metformin, vancomycin, DOACs: renally cleared; need dose adjustment.
Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (erythromycin, fluconazole, diltiazem, grapefruit juice) raise eplerenone but not spironolactone levels.
RALES showed spironolactone helps severe heart failure on an ACE inhibitor — afterward hyperkalemia admissions and deaths rose.

children.name: Pharmacokinetics
facts: Acetazolamide diuresis fades within 2–3 days (reduce dose in renal insufficiency); mannitol must be given IV — orally it causes osmotic diarrhea.

children.name: Monitoring
facts: Spironolactone: monitor potassium and creatinine within 1 week; life-threatening hyperkalemia, especially in CKD or with ACE inhibitor/ARB.
Mannitol: monitor osmolality and electrolytes.

children.name: Clinical pearls / "why" hook
facts: Case: a patient with stage 3 chronic kidney disease and heart failure is taking an ACE inhibitor and is started on spironolactone for additional heart-failure benefit; two weeks later a routine basic metabolic panel shows potassium 6.1 mEq/L.
**What is the mechanistic explanation for this finding, and what does it suggest about future drug combinations in this unit?**

**Both the ACE inhibitor (by reducing aldosterone) and spironolactone (by directly blocking the aldosterone receptor) independently reduce potassium excretion — combined, and in the setting of CKD (which already impairs potassium excretion), the hyperkalemia risk compounds.**
**This is the same additive-risk logic that will reappear as the "triple whammy" in Session 2.** The ACEi/aldosterone-antagonist pair is one of three “whammies” formalized next session.

Recap: diuretic classes are organized by nephron site (Figure 2): loop diuretics (thick ascending limb) are most potent, followed by thiazides (distal tubule), then potassium-sparing and carbonic anhydrase inhibitors.
Recap: loop and thiazide diuretics have opposite effects on calcium excretion (Figure 3); potassium-sparing diuretics carry a hyperkalemia risk that compounds with ACE inhibitors or ARBs.

Session 2 (Thursday, November 19) continues with antihypertensive therapy in chronic kidney disease and the cardiovascular-renal overlap, including vasodilators and angina pharmacology — RAAS blockers and the triple whammy first.
SGLT2 inhibitors block proximal glucose and Na⁺ reabsorption; main indication now cardiorenal protection. Adverse reactions: sixfold genital fungal infections in women, initial GFR dip.
Antidiuretic hormone antagonists (vaptans): oral tolvaptan (V2), IV conivaptan (V1a and V2) for SIADH when water restriction fails; watch sodium and liver tests.

hy: Falling GFR → accumulation → toxicity: cut the maintenance dose, stretch the interval, or both; check CrCl first.
Sodium reabsorbed: proximal ~65%, loop ~25%, distal 5–8%, collecting duct 2–3%.
Loop = NKCC2, thick ascending limb, most potent, ↑ Ca²⁺ excretion, ototoxicity. Thiazide = NCC, DCT, first-line HTN, ↓ Ca²⁺ excretion.
Thiazides fade below GFR ~30 → switch to a loop.
Potassium-sparing: aldosterone antagonists (spironolactone, eplerenone) and ENaC blockers (amiloride, triamterene); hyperkalemia worsens with ACEi/ARB or CKD.
Acetazolamide = glaucoma, altitude sickness, alkalosis; mannitol = ICP/IOP.
